# React Native JSI Deep Dive — Part 1: React Native Architecture — Threads, Hermes, and the Event Loop


"The most dangerous thought you can have as a creative person is to think you know what you're doing."

— Bret Victor, The Future of Programming, 2013


Excerpt: You've built React Native apps for years. You know `useState`, you know `FlatList`, you know how to call a native module. But do you know what happens in the 16 milliseconds between your `onPress` handler and the pixel changing on screen? Three execution threads, two runtime environments (JavaScript via Hermes, native via Objective-C/Java/C++), and a message-passing architecture that explains every performance problem you've ever had.


Series: React Native JSI Deep Dive (12 parts)

Part 1: React Native Architecture — Threads, Hermes, and the Event Loop (You are here) | Part 2: React Native Bridge vs JSI — What Changed and Why | Part 3: C++ for JavaScript Developers | Part 4: Your First React Native JSI Function | Part 5: HostObjects — Exposing C++ Classes to JavaScript | Part 6: Memory Ownership | Part 7: Platform Wiring | Part 8: Threading & Async | Part 9: Audio Pipeline | Part 10: Storage Engine | Part 11: Module Approaches | Part 12: Debugging


## The Crash

Before we begin — read this. It's a production crash report from an Android audio calling app built with React Native and JSI. The app worked perfectly for months, then started crashing when users backgrounded it during a call.


```
*** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** ***
pid: 14329, tid: 14412 (AudioEncoder), name: com.callingapp
signal 11 (SIGSEGV), code 1 (SEGV_MAPERR), fault addr 0x7b1a4fe000

backtrace:
      #00 pc 0x00004a8c4  /apex/.../bionic/libc.so (memcpy+180)
      #01 pc 0x000018f30  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (audio::TxRingBuffer::push(uint8_t const*, unsigned long, long)+160)
      #02 pc 0x00001c244  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (audio::CaptureEncoderThread::processFrame(audio::CaptureQueue&)+308)
      #03 pc 0x00001bc80  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (audio::CaptureEncoderThread::run()+192)
      #04 pc 0x0000b7e48  /apex/.../bionic/libc.so (__pthread_start(void*)+208)

  --- thread 14329: main ---
      #00 pc 0x000aee14  /apex/.../bionic/libc.so (__epoll_pwait+8)
      #01 pc 0x00017630  /system/lib64/libutils.so (android::Looper::pollOnce(int)+188)

  --- thread 14358: mqt_js ---
      #00 pc 0x003c7a90  /data/.../lib/arm64/libhermes.so
              (facebook::hermes::vm::Hades::collectOG()+1280)
      #01 pc 0x003a4c24  /data/.../lib/arm64/libhermes.so
              (facebook::hermes::vm::GCBase::finalizeUnreachableObjects()+172)
      #02 pc 0x000018240  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (std::__ndk1::shared_ptr::~shared_ptr()+48)
      #03 pc 0x000017b60  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (audio::AudioPipelineHostObject::~AudioPipelineHostObject()+64)
      #04 pc 0x00001a380  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (audio::TxRingBuffer::~TxRingBuffer()+32)
      #05 pc 0x003c28f4  /data/.../lib/arm64/libhermes.so
              (facebook::jsi::Runtime::PointerValue::invalidate()+28)
```

You probably can't read most of this yet. That's the point.


By the end of this series, you'll understand every line — which thread crashed, what it was doing, which memory system freed the bytes it was reading, why the garbage collector and C++ destructor disagreed about who owns a buffer, and how to fix it. Each post decodes a few more frames. By Part 12, you'll read this trace the way a mechanic reads an engine code.


For now, file it away. We'll come back to it.


## The Hidden Architecture: Three Threads, Two Runtimes

Here's something that should bother you: when you write a React Native component, it feels like you're writing a single program.


App.tsx

```
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
     setCount(count + 1)}>
      {count}
    
  );
}
```

One file. One function. One mental model: user taps, state changes, screen updates. It feels no different from a web app.


But this is an illusion. When you press that button, your tap crosses three execution threads, passes through two runtime environments — JavaScript (Hermes) and native (Objective-C/Java/C++) — and triggers a cascade of messages between worlds that don't share memory, don't share a clock, and barely speak the same language.


Every performance problem you've ever encountered in React Native — janky scrolling, delayed touch responses, slow native module calls, mysterious frame drops — traces back to this three-thread architecture. Understanding the React Native architecture doesn't just explain the problems. It makes the solutions feel inevitable.


## The Three Threads

React Native is not a single-threaded JavaScript application that talks to native views. It behaves like a distributed system running on your phone — independent execution domains communicating via message passing. The official architecture docs focus on two primary threads — JS and UI — though Fabric also uses background threads for layout. In practice, native module work runs on additional background thread pools, making the effective model three execution domains. In the New Architecture, the Fabric renderer may use additional threads for layout and shadow tree operations, but the JS/UI/Background mental model remains the most useful conceptual starting point.


### Thread 1: JavaScript

This is where your code runs. Your components, your hooks, your business logic, your API calls — all of it executes here, inside a JavaScript engine.


In modern React Native (default since 0.70), that engine is Hermes — a JavaScript VM designed specifically for React Native. Unlike V8 in Chrome — which interprets bytecode via its Ignition interpreter, baseline-compiles all functions through Sparkplug, then selectively optimizes hot code paths through Maglev and TurboFan — Hermes takes a different approach. The Hermes compiler (`hermesc`) pre-compiles your JavaScript to bytecode as a build step after Metro bundles the JS. The app ships this pre-compiled bytecode. When the app starts, Hermes executes it directly — no parsing, no JIT compilation, no warm-up.


Terminology: Hermes is a JavaScript engine optimized for React Native. It uses ahead-of-time bytecode compilation (via `hermesc` as a post-bundling build step), a concurrent generational garbage collector (Hades), and a memory model tuned for mobile constraints. It's not V8 (Chrome) or JavaScriptCore (Safari) — it's purpose-built.


The JS thread has one event loop, just like a browser. When your `onPress` handler fires, it goes into the event loop queue. When a `fetch` response arrives, its callback goes into the queue. When a timer fires, same queue. One thread processes them one at a time, in order.


This means JavaScript is fundamentally single-threaded. While your event handler runs, nothing else happens on this thread. No other callback fires. No state update processes. If your handler takes 100ms (say, sorting a large array), the UI is frozen for those 100ms — not because the screen can't update, but because the JS thread is busy and can't process the next item in the queue.


### Thread 2: UI (Main Thread)

This is the platform's main thread — the one that actually draws pixels and handles touch events. On iOS, it's the thread that runs UIKit. On Android, it's the one that runs the View system.


The UI thread has one overriding constraint: it must submit work to the rendering pipeline within the frame budget — 16.6ms (60fps) or 8.3ms (120fps on newer devices). If it misses a frame, the user sees a stutter. If it misses several, the interface feels broken.


This thread does not run JavaScript. It runs native platform code — view hierarchy updates, animation interpolations, touch hit-testing. (In the New Architecture, layout calculations via Yoga happen during Fabric's commit phase on a background thread, not the UI thread.) Your React components don't exist here. What exists here are native views — `UIView` on iOS, `android.view.View` on Android — that React Native's rendering system creates and manages on your behalf.


Key Insight: When you write `<Text>Hello</Text>` in React Native, no `Text` component exists on the UI thread. Instead, React Native creates a native platform view — on iOS, a custom `UIView` subclass (`RCTParagraphComponentView` in Fabric) that uses TextKit for rendering; on Android, a custom `View` subclass. These are real native views that the operating system knows how to composite. Your React tree is a description of what the UI should look like. The UI thread holds the reality.


### Thread 3: Native Modules (Background)

The third thread — or more accurately, a pool of background threads — handles native module work. When your JavaScript calls `AsyncStorage.getItem('key')`, the work doesn't happen on the JS thread or the UI thread. It's dispatched to a background thread where native code reads from disk, then the result is sent back to the JS thread.


This is where native modules live: camera access, file I/O, biometric auth, Bluetooth — anything that talks to platform APIs.


## How They Talk: Messages, Not Memory

Here's the critical insight: in the old architecture, these three threads did not share memory — they communicated exclusively by passing serialized messages. The New Architecture changes this partially: Fabric uses shared immutable C++ data structures (like the shadow tree) that multiple threads can read, and JSI allows the JS thread to directly invoke C++ code. But the core principle still holds — threads coordinate through well-defined interfaces, not by reading each other's mutable state, and most cross-thread communication still follows a message-passing pattern.


Think of three people in separate rooms. In the old architecture, the rooms were soundproof — you slid notes under the door. In the New Architecture, some rooms have a shared read-only bulletin board (the immutable shadow tree) and a direct intercom (JSI) — but you still can't reach in and rearrange someone else's desk.


```
┌─────────────┐     messages     ┌─────────────┐     messages     ┌─────────────┐
│             │    ──────────▶   │             │    ──────────▶   │             │
│  JS Thread  │                  │  UI Thread  │                  │   Native    │
│  (Hermes)   │    ◀──────────   │  (UIKit /   │    ◀──────────   │   Modules   │
│             │     messages     │   Android)  │     messages     │             │
└─────────────┘                  └─────────────┘                  └─────────────┘
```

When your `onPress` handler calls `setCount(count + 1)`, here's the actual sequence:


- JS thread: React runs your handler, computes the new virtual DOM, diffs it against the previous one, and determines that the `Text` component's content changed from "0" to "1".

- JS thread → UI thread: React Native dispatches an update: "Update the text property of native view #42 to '1'."

- UI thread: Receives the update, finds native view #42, updates its text property, and includes it in the next frame render.


The user sees "1" on screen. For a simple update like this, the pipeline typically completes within a single frame (~16ms at 60fps). But if either thread is busy — the JS thread running expensive computation, or the UI thread compositing a complex animation — the update can be delayed across multiple frames.


Feynman Moment: The soundproof rooms analogy is useful but breaks in an important way. Real soundproof rooms have a fixed door — you always pass notes through the same slot. In React Native, the mechanism for passing notes changed completely between the old and new architecture. The old architecture used a JSON serialization bridge (slow, asynchronous). The New Architecture — which includes Bridgeless Mode, replacing the old JSON bridge — uses JSI, a C++ interface that lets the rooms share certain objects directly. That's what the rest of this series is about.


## Let's Trace a Button Press

Here's the full path a tap takes through the system — from finger to pixel:


```
User Tap
   │
   ▼
UI Thread (touch hit-testing)
   │
   ▼
EventDispatcher → JSI
   │
   ▼
JS Thread (onPress handler)
   │
   ▼
React reconciliation (diff)
   │
   ▼
Fabric commit
   │
   ▼
UI Thread (native view update)
   │
   ▼
Next frame render → pixel changes
```

Let's walk through each step. (The timing estimates below are illustrative — actual durations vary by device, load, and complexity. No official benchmarks publish sub-millisecond breakdowns for this path.)


Touch begins. The user's finger contacts the screen. The operating system detects this on the UI thread and begins hit-testing: which native view is under the finger?


Touch dispatched. The UI thread identifies the native `TouchableOpacity` view and dispatches the event through React Native's `EventDispatcher`, which delivers it to the JavaScript runtime: "Touch began at coordinates (x, y) on view #37." (In the New Architecture, this delivery goes through JSI rather than the legacy bridge.)


JS processes the event. The JS thread picks up the event from its event loop queue. React's event system maps view #37 to your `onPress` callback. Your handler runs: `setCount(count + 1)`.


React reconciliation. React runs the component again with the new state. It diffs the new virtual DOM against the previous one. It finds one change: the `Text` node's children changed from "0" to "1".


Fabric commit. React Native's rendering system — Fabric — packages the change and commits it. Fabric is the modern renderer that replaced the legacy UIManager; it coordinates layout and mounting between the JS and UI threads. The commit: "Set property 'text' to '1' on shadow node #42."


UI thread applies the update. The UI thread receives the update, modifies the native view, and marks the view hierarchy as needing a redraw.


Next frame. The OS composites the updated view hierarchy into the next display frame. The user sees "1".


For a simple counter, the entire pipeline typically completes within a single frame (~16ms at 60fps). The JS thread does its work quickly — reconciliation for a single text change takes well under a millisecond on modern devices. The rest is coordination: waiting for the event to reach JS, waiting for the commit to reach the UI thread, waiting for the next frame boundary.


Now imagine what happens when those 4ms of JS work become 40ms. Or when the UI thread is busy running a complex animation. Or when a native module call inserts another round trip. The messages pile up, the threads fall out of sync, and the user feels the lag.


## The Event Loop (Your Friend and Your Bottleneck)

The JS thread runs a single event loop. Everything — touch handlers, timers, network callbacks, native module results — enters the same queue and is processed one at a time.


```
Event Loop Queue:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ onPress() │ setTimeout() │ fetch() callback │ ... │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     ▲                                        │
     │         Process one at a time           │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

This is conceptually similar to how browsers process JavaScript tasks. And it has the same fundamental implication: any single task that takes too long blocks everything behind it.


Blocking the event loop

```
function onPress() {
  // This blocks the entire JS thread for ~200ms
  const sorted = hugeArray.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));
  setData(sorted);
}
```

While `sort()` runs, no touch events are processed, no animations are driven from JS, no network callbacks fire, no timers execute. The app appears frozen — not because the UI thread is stuck (it's still rendering the old state perfectly smoothly), but because the JS thread can't tell it to change anything.


Gotcha: This is why React Native animations should avoid running on the JS thread. With the core `Animated` API, set `useNativeDriver: true` to run animations entirely on the UI thread. With Reanimated (the dominant animation library in production RN apps), animations run as worklets on the UI thread via JSI — no `useNativeDriver` flag needed. Either way, the principle is the same: a JS-driven animation means the JS thread must send a position update to the UI thread every 16ms. If the JS thread is busy, it misses frames and the animation stutters. A UI-thread animation doesn't need JS to participate at all.


## How Hermes Works: Bytecode, Hades GC, and jsi::Runtime

The JS thread doesn't run JavaScript directly. It runs Hermes, a JavaScript engine with several properties that matter for React Native:


### Bytecode Compilation

V8 in Chrome parses JavaScript source code at runtime, interprets it as bytecode (via Ignition), and then selectively JIT-compiles frequently-executed code paths through multiple optimization tiers (Sparkplug, Maglev, TurboFan). Hermes skips all of this at runtime. The `hermesc` compiler compiles JavaScript to bytecode as a build step — after Metro bundles your JS, but before the app is packaged. The app ships Hermes bytecode, not JavaScript source.


```
V8 (Chrome):     Source code → Parse → AST → Bytecode → Interpret (Ignition)
                  [hot paths only] → JIT compile (Sparkplug/Maglev/TurboFan) → Machine code
                  (parsing + interpretation at runtime; JIT warms up over time)

Hermes (RN):     Source code → hermesc → Bytecode (at build time)
                  Bytecode → Execute directly (at runtime — fast startup)
```

This is why React Native apps with Hermes start faster: there's no parsing step when the app launches. The tradeoff is that Hermes executes bytecode directly without a JIT compiler — no runtime compilation to native machine code. This improves startup time and memory usage at the cost of peak compute performance compared to JIT engines like V8. For most React Native workloads (UI-driven, event-based, not compute-heavy), direct bytecode execution is fast enough. For compute-heavy work, you should be in native code anyway — which is exactly what this series teaches.


### The Hades Garbage Collector

Hermes uses a mostly-concurrent generational garbage collector called Hades. "Mostly-concurrent" means it performs the bulk of collection work on a background thread while your JavaScript is running — but it still requires brief stop-the-world pauses for specific phases like root marking and weak reference finalization. "Generational" means it separates objects into young and old generations — young objects (recently allocated, likely short-lived) are collected frequently and cheaply, while old objects (survived multiple collections) are collected less often. (Historically, on 32-bit platforms, Hades ran in incremental mode rather than concurrent — though 32-bit targets are increasingly rare in modern React Native.)


This matters because GC pauses are one of the most common causes of frame drops in JavaScript applications. Hermes's predecessor GC (GenGC) used a traditional generational approach with stop-the-world pauses that could be significant on large heaps. Hades aims to reduce pause times by roughly an order of magnitude compared to GenGC by doing most work concurrently, though actual pauses depend on heap size and device.


Key Insight: Hades is one reason React Native 0.76+ feels smoother than older versions. JavaScriptCore (the previous default engine) has its own concurrent GC (Riptide, introduced in 2017), but Hermes's GC is specifically tuned for mobile constraints — optimizing for memory footprint and startup time rather than peak throughput. The combination of AOT bytecode (no parse/compile at startup) and Hades (short GC pauses) gives Hermes a clear edge on mobile devices.


### The jsi::Runtime Interface

Here's where things get interesting for the rest of this series. Hermes doesn't just run JavaScript — it exposes a C++ interface called `jsi::Runtime` that native code can use to interact with the JavaScript world.

29	## The Problem: Your C++ Compiles. Now Ship It.

32

34	cpp/install.cpp — our starting point from Part 4

37	#include 
38	
39	using namespace facebook;
40	
41	void install(jsi::Runtime& rt) {
42	    auto add = jsi::Function::createFromHostFunction(
43	        rt,
44	        jsi::PropNameID::forAscii(rt, "nativeAdd"),
45	        2,
46	        [](jsi::Runtime& rt, const jsi::Value& thisVal,
47	           const jsi::Value* args, size_t count) -> jsi::Value {
48	            double a = args[0].asNumber();
49	            double b = args[1].asNumber();

# React Native JSI Deep Dive — Part 7: Platform Wiring — Shipping C++ on iOS and Android


"The purpose of abstracting is not to be vague, but to create a new semantic level in which one can be absolutely precise."

— Edsger W. Dijkstra, The Humble Programmer, 1972


Excerpt: You've written C++ that talks to JavaScript. It works in your head, it compiles in isolation — but React Native runs on iOS and Android, and those platforms don't speak C++ natively. iOS speaks Objective-C. Android speaks Java. This post is the plumbing: how to wrap your C++ in the right language on each platform, configure the build systems, and wire everything so your `install()` function runs at the right moment on app startup.


Series: React Native JSI Deep Dive (12 parts)

Part 1: Runtime Architecture | Part 2: Bridge vs JSI | Part 3: C++ Foundations | Part 4: JSI Functions | Part 5: HostObjects | Part 6: Memory Ownership | Part 7: Platform Wiring (You are here) | Part 8: Threading & Async | Part 9: Audio Pipeline | Part 10: Storage Engine | Part 11: Module Approaches | Part 12: Debugging


## Quick Recap

In Part 4, we wrote an `install()` function that registers C++ host functions into the JavaScript runtime. In Part 5, we built HostObjects — full C++ classes exposed to JavaScript. In Part 6, we mapped the memory boundary between GC and native heap.


All of that code starts with the same assumption: someone gives us a `jsi::Runtime&`. But who? Where does the runtime come from? And how does the operating system know to compile and load your C++ in the first place?


That's what this post answers. This is the plumbing that turns `.cpp` files into a working native module on real devices.


## The Problem: Your C++ Compiles. Now Ship It.

Let's revisit the `install` function from Part 4:


cpp/install.cpp — our starting point from Part 4

```
#include 

using namespace facebook;

void install(jsi::Runtime& rt) {
    auto add = jsi::Function::createFromHostFunction(
        rt,
        jsi::PropNameID::forAscii(rt, "nativeAdd"),
        2,
        [](jsi::Runtime& rt, const jsi::Value& thisVal,
           const jsi::Value* args, size_t count) -> jsi::Value {
            double a = args[0].asNumber();
            double b = args[1].asNumber();
            return jsi::Value(a + b);
        }
    );
    rt.global().setProperty(rt, "nativeAdd", std::move(add));
}
```

This code is platform-agnostic. It uses only `jsi::Runtime`, which is a C++ abstract class defined in React Native's `jsi.h` header. It compiles identically on iOS and Android.


But this function doesn't run itself. Three problems stand between it and the user's phone:


- Compilation. iOS uses Xcode and Clang. Android uses the NDK and CMake. Each build system needs to know where your `.cpp` files are, what headers to find, and what libraries to link against.

- Language bridging. iOS's AppDelegate is Objective-C. Android's ReactPackage is Java/Kotlin. Neither can call a C++ function directly — you need a thin layer of glue code on each platform.

- Initialization timing. Your `install()` must run after the runtime exists but before JavaScript tries to call `nativeAdd()`. Get the timing wrong and you get either a crash or an undefined function.


```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Your C++ Code                            │
│                                                              │
│  install(jsi::Runtime& rt) { ... }                           │
│                                                              │
│  ✓ Platform-agnostic    ✓ Compiles anywhere                  │
│  ✗ Nothing calls it     ✗ Nothing compiles it                │
└──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                           │
              ┌────────────┴────────────┐
              │                         │
              ▼                         ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐
│   iOS Platform Layer    │ │  Android Platform Layer  │
│                         │ │                          │
│  Objective-C++ (.mm)    │ │  JNI + Java/Kotlin       │
│  CocoaPods / Podspec    │ │  CMake + Gradle          │
│  Xcode build system     │ │  NDK build system        │
│                         │ │                          │
│  Gets runtime from      │ │  Gets runtime from       │
│  RCTCxxBridge           │ │  JavaScriptContextHolder │
│  (+ Bridgeless shim)    │ │  via JNI                 │
└─────────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────┘
```

Figure 1: One C++ core, two platform-specific wiring layers. The C++ code is portable — the build systems and initialization code are not.


This is the "platform wiring" — the two per-platform layers that compile your C++, bridge the language gap, and call `install()` at the right time.


## The Mental Model: One Engine, Two Assembly Lines

Think of your C++ `install()` function as a car engine. It's the same engine regardless of what car it goes into. But a Toyota factory and a BMW factory have completely different assembly lines — different robots, different conveyor belts, different quality checks. The engine doesn't care. But it won't drive without the assembly line putting it in a car.


iOS's assembly line uses Objective-C++ — a hybrid language that can call both Objective-C (for Apple frameworks) and C++ (for your JSI code) in the same file. The build system is CocoaPods feeding into Xcode.


Android's assembly line uses JNI (Java Native Interface) — a C API that lets Java/Kotlin call C++ functions. The build system is CMake (for C++) feeding into Gradle (for Java/Kotlin).


Feynman Moment: Here's the key insight. C++ promises "write once, compile anywhere." It delivers on the compile part — the same `.cpp` file compiles on both platforms. But nobody told the build systems. Xcode doesn't read `CMakeLists.txt`. Gradle doesn't read podspecs. The C++ is portable. The plumbing around it is not. That's the tax you pay for native access: one C++ core, two sets of wiring, maintained in parallel.


## The File Layout

Before we dive into each platform, here's the directory structure of a JSI native module that ships on both iOS and Android. Every production JSI library — react-native-mmkv, react-native-reanimated, VisionCamera — follows this pattern:


```
react-native-my-module/
├── cpp/                          # Shared C++ — platform-agnostic
│   ├── install.h                 # Declaration: void install(jsi::Runtime& rt)
│   └── install.cpp               # Implementation: host functions, HostObjects
│
├── MyModule.podspec              # CocoaPods build configuration (at root)
├── ios/                          # iOS-specific wiring
│   ├── MyModule.h                # Obj-C++ header
│   └── MyModule.mm               # Obj-C++ implementation (calls install())
│
├── android/                      # Android-specific wiring
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt            # CMake build configuration for C++
│   ├── src/main/java/com/.../
│   │   ├── MyModulePackage.kt    # ReactPackage — registers the module
│   │   └── MyModule.kt           # Kotlin class with JNI native method
│   └── build.gradle              # Gradle build (links CMake, dependencies)
│
├── src/                          # TypeScript/JavaScript API
│   └── index.ts                  # Public API the app imports
│
└── package.json                  # npm package metadata
```

The key principle: `cpp/` contains zero platform-specific code. It includes only `jsi/jsi.h` and standard C++ headers. Everything in `ios/` and `android/` exists solely to compile that C++ and call `install()` with the runtime.


## iOS: Objective-C++ and CocoaPods


### Why Objective-C++

iOS apps are built with Objective-C or Swift. React Native's internals are Objective-C++. Your JSI code is C++. You need a language that speaks both Objective-C (to interact with React Native's iOS layer) and C++ (to call your `install` function).


That language is Objective-C++. It's not a separate language — it's Objective-C with C++ support enabled. Any `.m` file renamed to `.mm` becomes Objective-C++. In the same file, you can write `[UIColor redColor]` (Objective-C) and `install(runtime)` (C++).


Key Insight: The `.mm` file extension is the entire trick on iOS. Rename `.m` to `.mm` and you can mix Objective-C and C++ freely. There's no import, no flag, no annotation — just the file extension.


### The JSI Installer

The iOS wiring needs to accomplish one thing: get a reference to the `jsi::Runtime` and pass it to your `install()` function.


The standard pattern uses `setBridge:`, which React Native calls on every module during initialization. This is a Bridge-era API — in Bridgeless mode (RN 0.76+), React Native calls `setBridge:` with an `RCTBridgeProxy` instead of a real `RCTCxxBridge`. The proxy exposes a `runtime` property through the interop layer, so the same code works in both modes. The code below uses a `respondsToSelector:` guard to verify the runtime is accessible before using it.


Here's the pattern:


ios/MyModule.mm — JSI installer (works in Bridge and Bridgeless mode)

```
#import "MyModule.h"
#import 
#import 
#import "install.h"  // ← your shared C++ header

using namespace facebook;

@implementation MyModule

@synthesize bridge = _bridge;

RCT_EXPORT_MODULE()  // registers this class with React Native

+ (BOOL)requiresMainQueueSetup {
    return YES;
}

// Called by React Native during module initialization.
// In Bridge mode, bridge is the real RCTCxxBridge.
// In Bridgeless mode (RN 0.76+), bridge is an RCTBridgeProxy.
- (void)setBridge:(RCTBridge *)bridge {
    _bridge = bridge;

    // Guard: check that the bridge exposes a runtime property.
    // In Bridge mode this is RCTCxxBridge; in Bridgeless mode (0.76+)
    // this is RCTBridgeProxy which also exposes runtime via the
    // interop layer. The C-style cast below only affects the compiler —
    // ObjC message dispatch is dynamic (objc_msgSend), so .runtime
    // dispatches to whichever class the object actually is.
    if (![bridge respondsToSelector:@selector(runtime)]) return;

    RCTCxxBridge *cxxBridge = (RCTCxxBridge *)bridge;

    jsi::Runtime *runtime = (jsi::Runtime *)cxxBridge.runtime;
    if (runtime == nullptr) return;

    // Call your platform-agnostic C++ install function
    install(*runtime);
}

@end
```

ios/MyModule.h

```
#import 

@interface MyModule : NSObject 
@end
```

Let's trace what happens:


- React Native starts up and creates the Hermes runtime.

- React Native loads registered modules. `RCT_EXPORT_MODULE()` ensures `MyModule` is in the list.

- React Native calls `setBridge:` on the module, passing the bridge object.

- The `respondsToSelector:` guard confirms the bridge exposes a `runtime` property. We extract the `jsi::Runtime*`.

- We call `install(*runtime)` — your platform-agnostic C++ function from `cpp/install.cpp`.

- From this point forward, JavaScript can call `nativeAdd()`.


Gotcha: The runtime pointer from `cxxBridge.runtime` is a `void*`. You must cast it to `jsi::Runtime*`. This is an intentional design choice — Objective-C headers can't include C++ types. The `respondsToSelector:` guard above is critical — it checks that the bridge object actually has a `runtime` property before accessing it. The C-style cast `(RCTCxxBridge *)bridge` looks unsafe, but in Objective-C it's a compiler hint only — message dispatch (`objc_msgSend`) always uses the object's actual class, so `.runtime` calls the right implementation whether the object is an `RCTCxxBridge` or an `RCTBridgeProxy`.


### The Podspec

The podspec tells CocoaPods how to compile your C++ files and where to find headers. This is the iOS equivalent of a `CMakeLists.txt`:


MyModule.podspec — at library root

```
require 'json'
package = JSON.parse(File.read(File.join(__dir__, 'package.json')))

Pod::Spec.new do |s|
  s.name         = package['name']
  s.version      = package['version']
  s.summary      = package['description']
  s.homepage     = package['homepage']
  s.license      = package['license']
  s.author       = package['author']
  s.source       = { :git => package['repository']['url'], :tag => s.version }

  s.ios.deployment_target = '15.1'

  # Source files (paths relative to this podspec — the library root)
  s.source_files = [
    'ios/**/*.{h,m,mm}',           # iOS wiring (Obj-C++ files)
    'cpp/**/*.{h,cpp}',            # Shared C++ (platform-agnostic)
  ]

  # Header search paths so #include "install.h" resolves
  s.pod_target_xcconfig = {
    'HEADER_SEARCH_PATHS' => '"$(PODS_TARGET_SRCROOT)/cpp"',
    'CLANG_CXX_LANGUAGE_STANDARD' => 'c++17',
  }

  # React Native dependencies
  s.dependency 'React-Core'        # RCTBridge, RCTBridgeModule
  s.dependency 'React-jsi'         # jsi/jsi.h — JSI runtime headers
end
```

The critical lines:


Line
Purpose


`s.source_files`
Tells Xcode which files to compile. Paths are relative to the podspec location (library root). Includes both `ios/*.mm` and `cpp/*.cpp`.


`HEADER_SEARCH_PATHS`
Lets `#include "install.h"` find headers in the `cpp/` directory. `PODS_TARGET_SRCROOT` resolves to the library root.

4690	## The Bug: Two Sentences
4691	
4692	The GC destroyed the `AudioPipelineHostObject` (and its owned `TxRingBuffer`) on the JS thread, while the encoder thread was still writing to the ring buffer's backing memory via a raw pointer.
4693	
4694	
4695	The encoder held a raw pointer instead of a `shared_ptr`, so the ring buffer's lifetime was controlled solely by the GC — which didn't know the encoder thread existed.
4696	
4697	
4698	## The Fix
4699	
4700	The encoder thread must co-own the ring buffer. Two approaches, both correct:
4701	
4702	
4703	### Approach A: Shared Ownership
4704	
4705	Give the encoder thread its own `shared_ptr<TxRingBuffer>`:
4706	
4707	
4708	cpp/CaptureEncoderThread.h — the fix
4709	
4710	```
4711	class CaptureEncoderThread {
4712	public:
4713	    // Encoder holds a shared_ptr — buffer survives until
4714	    // BOTH the HostObject AND the encoder release it.
4715	    CaptureEncoderThread(std::shared_ptr txBuf)
4716	        : txBuf_(std::move(txBuf)) {}
4717	
4718	    void run() {
4719	        while (running_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
4720	            processFrame();
4721	        }
4722	    }
4723	
4724	private:
4725	    std::shared_ptr txBuf_;  // co-owns the buffer
4726	    std::atomic running_{true};
4727	
4728	    void processFrame() {
4729	        // ... encode audio ...
4730	        txBuf_->push(encoded.data(), encoded.size(), timestamp);
4731	    }
4732	};
4733	```
4734	
4735	When the GC destroys the HostObject, the HostObject's `shared_ptr` drops — but the encoder's `shared_ptr` keeps the ring buffer alive. The buffer is freed only after the encoder thread stops and releases its `shared_ptr`. No dangling pointer. No SIGSEGV.
4736	
4737	
4738	### Approach B: Coordinated Shutdown
4739	
4740	The HostObject's destructor stops the encoder thread before freeing resources:
4741	
4742	
4743	cpp/AudioPipelineHostObject.h — alternative fix
4744	
4745	```
4746	class AudioPipelineHostObject : public jsi::HostObject {
4747	public:
4748	    ~AudioPipelineHostObject() {
4749	        // Signal the encoder to stop
4750	        encoder_->stop();  // sets running_ = false
4751	
4752	        // Wait for it to finish — no more push() calls after this
4753	        encoderThread_.join();
4754	
4755	        // Now safe to destroy the ring buffer (implicit via member destruction)
4756	    }
4757	
4758	private:
4759	    std::unique_ptr encoder_;
4760	    std::thread encoderThread_;
4761	    TxRingBuffer txBuf_;  // destroyed AFTER thread is joined
4762	};
4763	```
4764	
4765	The destructor body runs first — it stops the encoder and joins the thread. Only after the body completes does C++ destroy members in reverse declaration order (`txBuf_` first, then `encoderThread_`, then `encoder_`). By the time `txBuf_` is destroyed, the thread has already been joined — no thread is accessing the buffer.
4766	
4767	
4768	Key Insight: Both fixes enforce the same invariant: no thread accesses the ring buffer after it's freed. Approach A extends the buffer's lifetime (via `shared_ptr`). Approach B shortens the thread's lifetime (via `join`). In practice, production audio pipelines use Approach A — because `join()` in a destructor triggered by the GC blocks the JS thread. A blocked JS thread can't dispatch Fabric layout updates or process timers, effectively freezing the app until the encoder thread exits.

4771	## The Debugging Toolkit
4772	
4773	The crash trace above was readable because the build included debug symbols. In production, you often get stripped binaries and hex addresses. Here's how to turn those into actionable information.
4774

4776	### 1. Symbol Demangling
4777	
4778	C++ compilers mangle function names to encode namespaces, classes, argument types, and template parameters. The raw mangled name looks like:
4779

4782	REDACTED
4783	```

4785	Demangle it with `c++filt` (available in the Android NDK and Xcode):

4788	terminal

4790	```
4791	$ c++filt REDACTED
4792	audio::TxRingBuffer::push(unsigned char const*, unsigned long, long)
4793	```

4795	The crash trace in Part 1 already shows demangled names — Android's `debuggerd` demangles automatically when symbols are available. If you see mangled names, pipe them through `c++filt`.

4800	Each frame includes a `pc` (program counter) offset and a library path:

4880	### 5. Address Sanitizer (ASan) for Development
4881	
4882	The most powerful tool for catching use-after-free bugs before production is Address Sanitizer (ASan). ASan instruments every memory allocation and deallocation, detecting use-after-free, buffer overflow, and stack overflow at the point they happen — not at the crash that follows.
4883	
4884	
4885	Enable it in your `CMakeLists.txt` for debug builds:
4886	
4887	
4888	CMakeLists.txt — enabling ASan
4889	
4890	```
4891	if(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE STREQUAL "Debug")
4892	    target_compile_options(audio PRIVATE -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer)
4893	    target_link_options(audio PRIVATE -fsanitize=address)
4894	endif()
4895	```
4896	
4897	For iOS, enable ASan in the Xcode scheme: Product → Scheme → Edit Scheme → Run → Diagnostics → Address Sanitizer.
4898	
4899	
4900	With ASan enabled, the Part 1 crash would be caught immediately — not as a SIGSEGV with a cryptic address, but as a detailed report:
4901	
4902	
4903	```
4904	ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x7b1a4fe000
4905	  WRITE of size 160 at 0x7b1a4fe000 thread T3 (AudioEncoder)
4906	
4907	  #0 memcpy
4908	  #1 audio::TxRingBuffer::push(...)  TxRingBuffer.cpp:47
4909	  ...
4910	
4911	  previously freed by thread T1 (mqt_js):
4912	  #0 operator delete
4913	  #1 audio::TxRingBuffer::~TxRingBuffer()  TxRingBuffer.cpp:12
4914	  #2 audio::AudioPipelineHostObject::~AudioPipelineHostObject()
4915	  ...
4916	```

4918	ASan tells you what was freed, who freed it, and who accessed it afterward — all in one report. This is the tool that would have caught the Part 1 bug in development.

4920	
4921	Gotcha: ASan adds significant runtime overhead (2-3x slower, 2-3x more memory). Never ship with it enabled. Use it in development and CI, not in production builds.

4924	## The Pitfall Checklist
4925	
4926	Every native module bug in this series traces to one of five root causes. Before shipping a JSI native module, verify each one.
4927	
4928	
4929	### 1. Ownership: Who Outlives Whom?
4930	
4931	The Part 1 crash. A thread held a raw pointer to a resource whose lifetime was controlled by the GC.
4932	
4933	
4934	Check: For every raw pointer or reference in your native code, answer: what owns the pointee, and can the pointee be freed while this pointer is live? If the answer involves the GC (via a HostObject) and the pointer lives on a background thread, you need either `shared_ptr` co-ownership or thread `join()` before destruction.

5125	## Key Takeaways
5126	
5127	
5128	- Read crash traces bottom-up. The lowest frame is the entry point; the top frame is where it faulted. Thread names, library paths, and demangled symbols tell you which domain (JS, native, platform) and which component crashed.
5129	
5130	- Use-after-free is the dominant JSI crash class. It happens when the GC frees a HostObject while a background thread holds a raw pointer to its resources. Fix with `shared_ptr` co-ownership or thread `join()` before destruction.
5131	
5132	- Archive unstripped binaries with every release. Without matching symbols, `addr2line` and `atos` return nothing. Symbolication is the difference between "crash at 0x18f30" and "crash at TxRingBuffer.cpp:47."
5133	
5134	- Enable Address Sanitizer in development and CI. ASan catches use-after-free, buffer overflow, and stack overflow at the point they happen — with detailed reports showing who allocated, who freed, and who accessed afterward. The Part 1 crash would have been caught immediately.
5135	
5136	- Run the five-point checklist before shipping. Ownership (who outlives whom), threading (JSI confined to JS thread), memory (one system frees each allocation), platform (iOS/Android differences), lifecycle (init before use, shutdown before free).

# React Native JSI Deep Dive — Part 12: Production Debugging and Pitfalls — Why Did It Crash and How Do You Find Out?


"The most effective debugging tool is still careful thought, coupled with judiciously placed print statements."

— Brian Kernighan, Unix for Beginners, 1979


Excerpt: A SIGSEGV in production gives you a wall of hex addresses, mangled C++ symbols, and three threads pointing fingers at each other. This post — the series finale — takes the crash trace from Part 1, decodes every frame with the tools and concepts from the entire series, shows the fix, and builds a checklist for catching these bugs before they ship.


Series: React Native JSI Deep Dive (12 parts)

Part 1: Runtime Architecture | Part 2: Bridge vs JSI | Part 3: C++ Foundations | Part 4: JSI Functions | Part 5: HostObjects | Part 6: Memory Ownership | Part 7: Platform Wiring | Part 8: Threading & Async | Part 9: Audio Pipeline | Part 10: Storage Engine | Part 11: Module Approaches | Part 12: Production Debugging and Pitfalls (You are here)


## Quick Recap

Across 11 posts, we've built an understanding of React Native's native layer from the ground up — the runtime architecture, JSI functions, HostObjects, memory ownership, platform wiring, threading, and two production systems (an audio pipeline and a storage engine). Along the way, every post decoded one more layer of a production crash trace introduced in Part 1.


This post brings it all together. We decode the entire trace, show the fix, and then zoom out to the debugging tools and patterns that help you catch these bugs before your users do.


## The Full Trace, One Last Time

## Decoding the Trace: Frame by Frame

Let's walk through every piece, mapping each symbol to the concept from the series that explains it.


### The Signal


```
signal 11 (SIGSEGV), code 1 (SEGV_MAPERR), fault addr 0x7b1a4fe000
```


- SIGSEGV — the process tried to access memory it doesn't own. The OS killed it.

- SEGV_MAPERR — the fault address isn't mapped into the process's virtual address space. This distinguishes use-after-free (address was freed) from null dereference (`0x0`). The fault address `0x7b1a4fe000` is non-null and high — it was once valid memory.

- This is a use-after-free: the memory at that address was deallocated, then accessed.


### The Crashing Thread: AudioEncoder


```
#00  memcpy+180                          (libc.so)
#01  audio::TxRingBuffer::push(...)      (libaudio.so)
#02  audio::CaptureEncoderThread::processFrame(...)  (libaudio.so)
#03  audio::CaptureEncoderThread::run()  (libaudio.so)
#04  __pthread_start(void*)              (libc.so)

Reading bottom-up (the call stack grows downward):

`#04 __pthread_start`
The OS thread entry point. A `std::thread` was created, and this is where it begins execution.
Part 8

Part 9

Part 9

#01  android::Looper::pollOnce(int)   (libutils.so)

Part 1


## The Bug: Two Sentences

The GC destroyed the `AudioPipelineHostObject` (and its owned `TxRingBuffer`) on the JS thread, while the encoder thread was still writing to the ring buffer's backing memory via a raw pointer.


The encoder held a raw pointer instead of a `shared_ptr`, so the ring buffer's lifetime was controlled solely by the GC — which didn't know the encoder thread existed.


## The Fix

The encoder thread must co-own the ring buffer. Two approaches, both correct:


### Approach A: Shared Ownership

Give the encoder thread its own `shared_ptr<TxRingBuffer>`:


cpp/CaptureEncoderThread.h — the fix

```
class CaptureEncoderThread {
public:
    // Encoder holds a shared_ptr — buffer survives until
    // BOTH the HostObject AND the encoder release it.
    CaptureEncoderThread(std::shared_ptr txBuf)
        : txBuf_(std::move(txBuf)) {}

    void run() {
        while (running_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
            processFrame();
        }
    }

private:
    std::shared_ptr txBuf_;  // co-owns the buffer
    std::atomic running_{true};

    void processFrame() {
        // ... encode audio ...
        txBuf_->push(encoded.data(), encoded.size(), timestamp);
    }
};
```

When the GC destroys the HostObject, the HostObject's `shared_ptr` drops — but the encoder's `shared_ptr` keeps the ring buffer alive. The buffer is freed only after the encoder thread stops and releases its `shared_ptr`. No dangling pointer. No SIGSEGV.


### Approach B: Coordinated Shutdown

The HostObject's destructor stops the encoder thread before freeing resources:


cpp/AudioPipelineHostObject.h — alternative fix

```
class AudioPipelineHostObject : public jsi::HostObject {
public:
    ~AudioPipelineHostObject() {
        // Signal the encoder to stop
        encoder_->stop();  // sets running_ = false

        // Wait for it to finish — no more push() calls after this
        encoderThread_.join();

        // Now safe to destroy the ring buffer (implicit via member destruction)
    }

private:
    std::unique_ptr encoder_;
    std::thread encoderThread_;
    TxRingBuffer txBuf_;  // destroyed AFTER thread is joined
};
```

The destructor body runs first — it stops the encoder and joins the thread. Only after the body completes does C++ destroy members in reverse declaration order (`txBuf_` first, then `encoderThread_`, then `encoder_`). By the time `txBuf_` is destroyed, the thread has already been joined — no thread is accessing the buffer.


Key Insight: Both fixes enforce the same invariant: no thread accesses the ring buffer after it's freed. Approach A extends the buffer's lifetime (via `shared_ptr`). Approach B shortens the thread's lifetime (via `join`). In practice, production audio pipelines use Approach A — because `join()` in a destructor triggered by the GC blocks the JS thread. A blocked JS thread can't dispatch Fabric layout updates or process timers, effectively freezing the app until the encoder thread exits.


## The Debugging Toolkit

The crash trace above was readable because the build included debug symbols. In production, you often get stripped binaries and hex addresses. Here's how to turn those into actionable information.


### 1. Symbol Demangling

C++ compilers mangle function names to encode namespaces, classes, argument types, and template parameters. The raw mangled name looks like:


```
REDACTED
```

Demangle it with `c++filt` (available in the Android NDK and Xcode):


terminal

```
$ c++filt REDACTED
audio::TxRingBuffer::push(unsigned char const*, unsigned long, long)
```

The crash trace in Part 1 already shows demangled names — Android's `debuggerd` demangles automatically when symbols are available. If you see mangled names, pipe them through `c++filt`.


### 2. Address-to-Line Mapping

Each frame includes a `pc` (program counter) offset and a library path:


```
#01 pc 0x000018f30  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
```

To map this to a source file and line number, use `addr2line` from the Android NDK:


terminal

```
$ $ANDROID_NDK/toolchains/llvm/prebuilt/darwin-x86_64/bin/llvm-addr2line \
    -e app/build/intermediates/merged_native_libs/debug/out/lib/arm64-v8a/libaudio.so \
    -f 0x000018f30
audio::TxRingBuffer::push(unsigned char const*, unsigned long, long)
/Users/dev/audio-app/cpp/TxRingBuffer.cpp:47
```

Now you know exactly which line of `TxRingBuffer.cpp` contains the `memcpy` that faulted. For iOS, use `atos`:


terminal

```
$ atos -o AudioModule.framework.dSYM/Contents/Resources/DWARF/AudioModule \
    -arch arm64 -l 0x100000000 0x000018f30
```


Gotcha: This only works if you kept the unstripped `.so` (or `.dSYM` for iOS) from the exact build that crashed. If you ship a release build and strip symbols, archive the unstripped binaries alongside each release. Without the matching symbols, `addr2line` returns `??:0`.


### 3. Android's `ndk-stack`

For Android tombstones (the full crash dump), the `ndk-stack` tool automates symbolication:


terminal

```
$ adb logcat | ndk-stack -sym app/build/intermediates/merged_native_libs/debug/out/lib/arm64-v8a/
```

This reads the tombstone from logcat, finds the matching `.so` files in the symbol directory, and outputs the crash trace with file names and line numbers. Use it as your first step when a native crash appears in logcat.


### 4. Hermes Profiler for JS Thread Analysis

If the crash involves the JS thread (like our GC-triggered destruction), the Hermes sampling profiler can show what JavaScript code was running before the GC triggered:


App.js — enabling the Hermes sampling profiler

```
// HermesInternal is a global object provided by the Hermes engine
const Hermes = global.HermesInternal;

// Start sampling profiler
Hermes?.enableSamplingProfiler?.();

// ... reproduce the crash scenario ...

// Stop profiling — Hermes writes the profile to the app's cache directory
Hermes?.disableSamplingProfiler?.();
```

terminal — retrieve the profile from the device

```
# Pull the .cpuprofile from the app's cache directory
adb pull /data/user/0/com.yourapp/cache/sampling-profiler-*.cpuprofile .

# Open in Chrome DevTools → Performance tab → Load profile
```

This won't show the native crash itself, but it reveals which JavaScript code was running when the GC decided to collect the HostObject — helping you understand what dropped the last reference.


### 5. Address Sanitizer (ASan) for Development

The most powerful tool for catching use-after-free bugs before production is Address Sanitizer (ASan). ASan instruments every memory allocation and deallocation, detecting use-after-free, buffer overflow, and stack overflow at the point they happen — not at the crash that follows.


Enable it in your `CMakeLists.txt` for debug builds:


CMakeLists.txt — enabling ASan

```
if(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE STREQUAL "Debug")
    target_compile_options(audio PRIVATE -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer)
    target_link_options(audio PRIVATE -fsanitize=address)
endif()
```

For iOS, enable ASan in the Xcode scheme: Product → Scheme → Edit Scheme → Run → Diagnostics → Address Sanitizer.


With ASan enabled, the Part 1 crash would be caught immediately — not as a SIGSEGV with a cryptic address, but as a detailed report:


```
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x7b1a4fe000
  WRITE of size 160 at 0x7b1a4fe000 thread T3 (AudioEncoder)

  #0 memcpy
  #1 audio::TxRingBuffer::push(...)  TxRingBuffer.cpp:47
  ...

  previously freed by thread T1 (mqt_js):
  #0 operator delete
  #1 audio::TxRingBuffer::~TxRingBuffer()  TxRingBuffer.cpp:12
  #2 audio::AudioPipelineHostObject::~AudioPipelineHostObject()
  ...
```

ASan tells you what was freed, who freed it, and who accessed it afterward — all in one report. This is the tool that would have caught the Part 1 bug in development.


Gotcha: ASan adds significant runtime overhead (2-3x slower, 2-3x more memory). Never ship with it enabled. Use it in development and CI, not in production builds.


## The Pitfall Checklist

Every native module bug in this series traces to one of five root causes. Before shipping a JSI native module, verify each one.


### 1. Ownership: Who Outlives Whom?

The Part 1 crash. A thread held a raw pointer to a resource whose lifetime was controlled by the GC.


Check: For every raw pointer or reference in your native code, answer: what owns the pointee, and can the pointee be freed while this pointer is live? If the answer involves the GC (via a HostObject) and the pointer lives on a background thread, you need either `shared_ptr` co-ownership or thread `join()` before destruction.


Pattern

Fix

`CallInvoker` callback captures `jsi::Value`

### 2. Threading: Who Calls What from Where?

The `jsi::Runtime` is confined to the JS thread (Part 1). Every JSI call from a background thread is undefined behavior.

If you followed the whole series, you now think about React Native native modules the way a systems programmer does: threads, ownership, lifetimes, and the boundary between two memory worlds.


That's the real takeaway. Not any one API or pattern, but the mental model: JavaScript and C++ are two systems with different rules for memory, threading, and cleanup. Every bug at the boundary comes from those systems making incompatible assumptions. ## Key Takeaways


- Read crash traces bottom-up. The lowest frame is the entry point; the top frame is where it faulted. Thread names, library paths, and demangled symbols tell you which domain (JS, native, platform) and which component crashed.

- Use-after-free is the dominant JSI crash class. It happens when the GC frees a HostObject while a background thread holds a raw pointer to its resources. Fix with `shared_ptr` co-ownership or thread `join()` before destruction.

- Archive unstripped binaries with every release. Without matching symbols, `addr2line` and `atos` return nothing. Symbolication is the difference between "crash at 0x18f30" and "crash at TxRingBuffer.cpp:47."

- Enable Address Sanitizer in development and CI. ASan catches use-after-free, buffer overflow, and stack overflow at the point they happen — with detailed reports showing who allocated, who freed, and who accessed afterward. The Part 1 crash would have been caught immediately.

- Run the five-point checklist before shipping. Ownership (who outlives whom), threading (JSI confined to JS thread), memory (one system frees each allocation), platform (iOS/Android differences), lifecycle (init before use, shutdown before free).

# React Native JSI Deep Dive — Part 1: React Native Architecture — Threads, Hermes, and the Event Loop


"The most dangerous thought you can have as a creative person is to think you know what you're doing."

— Bret Victor, The Future of Programming, 2013


Excerpt: You've built React Native apps for years. You know `useState`, you know `FlatList`, you know how to call a native module. But do you know what happens in the 16 milliseconds between your `onPress` handler and the pixel changing on screen? Three execution threads, two runtime environments (JavaScript via Hermes, native via Objective-C/Java/C++), and a message-passing architecture that explains every performance problem you've ever had.


Series: React Native JSI Deep Dive (12 parts)

Part 1: React Native Architecture — Threads, Hermes, and the Event Loop (You are here) | Part 2: React Native Bridge vs JSI — What Changed and Why | Part 3: C++ for JavaScript Developers | Part 4: Your First React Native JSI Function | Part 5: HostObjects — Exposing C++ Classes to JavaScript | Part 6: Memory Ownership | Part 7: Platform Wiring | Part 8: Threading & Async | Part 9: Audio Pipeline | Part 10: Storage Engine | Part 11: Module Approaches | Part 12: Debugging


## The Crash

Before we begin — read this. It's a production crash report from an Android audio calling app built with React Native and JSI. The app worked perfectly for months, then started crashing when users backgrounded it during a call.


```
*** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** *** ***
pid: 14329, tid: 14412 (AudioEncoder), name: com.callingapp
signal 11 (SIGSEGV), code 1 (SEGV_MAPERR), fault addr 0x7b1a4fe000

backtrace:
      #00 pc 0x00004a8c4  /apex/.../bionic/libc.so (memcpy+180)
      #01 pc 0x000018f30  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (audio::TxRingBuffer::push(uint8_t const*, unsigned long, long)+160)
      #02 pc 0x00001c244  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (audio::CaptureEncoderThread::processFrame(audio::CaptureQueue&)+308)
      #03 pc 0x00001bc80  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (audio::CaptureEncoderThread::run()+192)
      #04 pc 0x0000b7e48  /apex/.../bionic/libc.so (__pthread_start(void*)+208)

  --- thread 14329: main ---
      #00 pc 0x000aee14  /apex/.../bionic/libc.so (__epoll_pwait+8)
      #01 pc 0x00017630  /system/lib64/libutils.so (android::Looper::pollOnce(int)+188)

  --- thread 14358: mqt_js ---
      #00 pc 0x003c7a90  /data/.../lib/arm64/libhermes.so
              (facebook::hermes::vm::Hades::collectOG()+1280)
      #01 pc 0x003a4c24  /data/.../lib/arm64/libhermes.so
              (facebook::hermes::vm::GCBase::finalizeUnreachableObjects()+172)
      #02 pc 0x000018240  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (std::__ndk1::shared_ptr::~shared_ptr()+48)
      #03 pc 0x000017b60  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (audio::AudioPipelineHostObject::~AudioPipelineHostObject()+64)
      #04 pc 0x00001a380  /data/.../lib/arm64/libaudio.so
              (audio::TxRingBuffer::~TxRingBuffer()+32)

              (facebook::jsi::Runtime::PointerValue::invalidate()+28)

You probably can't read most of this yet. That's the point.


By the end of this series, you'll understand every line — which thread crashed, what it was doing, which memory system freed the bytes it was reading, why the garbage collector and C++ destructor disagreed about who owns a buffer, and how to fix it. Each post decodes a few more frames. By Part 12, you'll read this trace the way a mechanic reads an engine code.


For now, file it away. We'll come back to it.


## The Hidden Architecture: Three Threads, Two Runtimes

Here's something that should bother you: when you write a React Native component, it feels like you're writing a single program.


App.tsx

```
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
     setCount(count + 1)}>
      {count}
    
  );
}
```

One file. One function. One mental model: user taps, state changes, screen updates. It feels no different from a web app.


But this is an illusion. When you press that button, your tap crosses three execution threads, passes through two runtime environments — JavaScript (Hermes) and native (Objective-C/Java/C++) — and triggers a cascade of messages between worlds that don't share memory, don't share a clock, and barely speak the same language.


Every performance problem you've ever encountered in React Native — janky scrolling, delayed touch responses, slow native module calls, mysterious frame drops — traces back to this three-thread architecture. Understanding the React Native architecture doesn't just explain the problems. It makes the solutions feel inevitable.


## The Three Threads

React Native is not a single-threaded JavaScript application that talks to native views. It behaves like a distributed system running on your phone — independent execution domains communicating via message passing. The official architecture docs focus on two primary threads — JS and UI — though Fabric also uses background threads for layout. In practice, native module work runs on additional background thread pools, making the effective model three execution domains. In the New Architecture, the Fabric renderer may use additional threads for layout and shadow tree operations, but the JS/UI/Background mental model remains the most useful conceptual starting point.


### Thread 1: JavaScript

This is where your code runs. Your components, your hooks, your business logic, your API calls — all of it executes here, inside a JavaScript engine.

1	=== PART 7 ===
2	# React Native JSI Deep Dive — Part 7: Platform Wiring — Shipping C++ on iOS and Android
3	
4	
5	"The purpose of abstracting is not to be vague, but to create a new semantic level in which one can be absolutely precise."
6	
7	— Edsger W. Dijkstra, The Humble Programmer, 1972
8	
9	
10	Excerpt: You've written C++ that talks to JavaScript. It works in your head, it compiles in isolation — but React Native runs on iOS and Android, and those platforms don't speak C++ natively. iOS speaks Objective-C. Android speaks Java. This post is the plumbing: how to wrap your C++ in the right language on each platform, configure the build systems, and wire everything so your `install()` function runs at the right moment on app startup.
11	
12	
13	Series: React Native JSI Deep Dive (12 parts)
14	
15	Part 1: Runtime Architecture | Part 2: Bridge vs JSI | Part 3: C++ Foundations | Part 4: JSI Functions | Part 5: HostObjects | Part 6: Memory Ownership | Part 7: Platform Wiring (You are here) | Part 8: Threading & Async | Part 9: Audio Pipeline | Part 10: Storage Engine | Part 11: Module Approaches | Part 12: Debugging
16	
17	
18	## Quick Recap
19	
20	In Part 4, we wrote an `install()` function that registers C++ host functions into the JavaScript runtime. In Part 5, we built HostObjects — full C++ classes exposed to JavaScript. In Part 6, we mapped the memory boundary between GC and native heap.
21	
22	
23	All of that code starts with the same assumption: someone gives us a `jsi::Runtime&`. But who? Where does the runtime come from? And how does the operating system know to compile and load your C++ in the first place?
24	
25	
26	That's what this post answers. This is the plumbing that turns `.cpp` files into a working native module on real devices.
27	
28	
29	## The Problem: Your C++ Compiles. Now Ship It.
30	
31	Let's revisit the `install` function from Part 4:
32	
33	
34	cpp/install.cpp — our starting point from Part 4
35	
36	```
37	#include 
38	
39	using namespace facebook;
40	
41	void install(jsi::Runtime& rt) {
42	    auto add = jsi::Function::createFromHostFunction(
43	        rt,
44	        jsi::PropNameID::forAscii(rt, "nativeAdd"),
45	        2,
46	        [](jsi::Runtime& rt, const jsi::Value& thisVal,
47	           const jsi::Value* args, size_t count) -> jsi::Value {
48	            double a = args[0].asNumber();
49	            double b = args[1].asNumber();
50	            return jsi::Value(a + b);
51	        }
52	    );
53	    rt.global().setProperty(rt, "nativeAdd", std::move(add));
54	}
55	```
56	
57	This code is platform-agnostic. It uses only `jsi::Runtime`, which is a C++ abstract class defined in React Native's `jsi.h` header. It compiles identically on iOS and Android.
58	
59	
60	But this function doesn't run itself. Three problems stand between it and the user's phone:
61	
62	
63	- Compilation. iOS uses Xcode and Clang. Android uses the NDK and CMake. Each build system needs to know where your `.cpp` files are, what headers to find, and what libraries to link against.
64	
65	- Language bridging. iOS's AppDelegate is Objective-C. Android's ReactPackage is Java/Kotlin. Neither can call a C++ function directly — you need a thin layer of glue code on each platform.
66	
67	- Initialization timing. Your `install()` must run after the runtime exists but before JavaScript tries to call `nativeAdd()`. Get the timing wrong and you get either a crash or an undefined function.
68	
69	
70	```
71	┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
72	│                     Your C++ Code                            │
73	│                                                              │
74	│  install(jsi::Runtime& rt) { ... }                           │
75	│                                                              │
76	│  ✓ Platform-agnostic    ✓ Compiles anywhere                  │
77	│  ✗ Nothing calls it     ✗ Nothing compiles it                │
78	└──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
79	                           │
80	              ┌────────────┴────────────┐
81	              │                         │
82	              ▼                         ▼
83	┌─────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐
84	│   iOS Platform Layer    │ │  Android Platform Layer  │
85	│                         │ │                          │
86	│  Objective-C++ (.mm)    │ │  JNI + Java/Kotlin       │
87	│  CocoaPods / Podspec    │ │  CMake + Gradle          │
88	│  Xcode build system     │ │  NDK build system        │
89	│                         │ │                          │
90	│  Gets runtime from      │ │  Gets runtime from       │
91	│  RCTCxxBridge           │ │  JavaScriptContextHolder │
92	│  (+ Bridgeless shim)    │ │  via JNI                 │
93	└─────────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────┘

=== PART 7 ===
# React Native JSI Deep Dive — Part 7: Platform Wiring — Shipping C++ on iOS and Android


"The purpose of abstracting is not to be vague, but to create a new semantic level in which one can be absolutely precise."

— Edsger W. Dijkstra, The Humble Programmer, 1972


Excerpt: You've written C++ that talks to JavaScript. It works in your head, it compiles in isolation — but React Native runs on iOS and Android, and those platforms don't speak C++ natively. iOS speaks Objective-C. Android speaks Java. This post is the plumbing: how to wrap your C++ in the right language on each platform, configure the build systems, and wire everything so your `install()` function runs at the right moment on app startup.


Series: React Native JSI Deep Dive (12 parts)

Part 1: Runtime Architecture | Part 2: Bridge vs JSI | Part 3: C++ Foundations | Part 4: JSI Functions | Part 5: HostObjects | Part 6: Memory Ownership | Part 7: Platform Wiring (You are here) | Part 8: Threading & Async | Part 9: Audio Pipeline | Part 10: Storage Engine | Part 11: Module Approaches | Part 12: Debugging


## Quick Recap

In Part 4, we wrote an `install()` function that registers C++ host functions into the JavaScript runtime. In Part 5, we built HostObjects — full C++ classes exposed to JavaScript. In Part 6, we mapped the memory boundary between GC and native heap.


All of that code starts with the same assumption: someone gives us a `jsi::Runtime&`. But who? Where does the runtime come from? And how does the operating system know to compile and load your C++ in the first place?


That's what this post answers. This is the plumbing that turns `.cpp` files into a working native module on real devices.


## The Problem: Your C++ Compiles. Now Ship It.

Let's revisit the `install` function from Part 4:


cpp/install.cpp — our starting point from Part 4

```
#include 

using namespace facebook;

void install(jsi::Runtime& rt) {
    auto add = jsi::Function::createFromHostFunction(
        rt,
        jsi::PropNameID::forAscii(rt, "nativeAdd"),
        2,
        [](jsi::Runtime& rt, const jsi::Value& thisVal,
           const jsi::Value* args, size_t count) -> jsi::Value {
            double a = args[0].asNumber();
            double b = args[1].asNumber();
            return jsi::Value(a + b);
        }
    );
    rt.global().setProperty(rt, "nativeAdd", std::move(add));
}
```

This code is platform-agnostic. It uses only `jsi::Runtime`, which is a C++ abstract class defined in React Native's `jsi.h` header. It compiles identically on iOS and Android.


But this function doesn't run itself. Three problems stand between it and the user's phone:


- Compilation. iOS uses Xcode and Clang. Android uses the NDK and CMake. Each build system needs to know where your `.cpp` files are, what headers to find, and what libraries to link against.

- Language bridging. iOS's AppDelegate is Objective-C. Android's ReactPackage is Java/Kotlin. Neither can call a C++ function directly — you need a thin layer of glue code on each platform.

- Initialization timing. Your `install()` must run after the runtime exists but before JavaScript tries to call `nativeAdd()`. Get the timing wrong and you get either a crash or an undefined function.


```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Your C++ Code                            │
│                                                              │
│  install(jsi::Runtime& rt) { ... }                           │
│                                                              │
│  ✓ Platform-agnostic    ✓ Compiles anywhere                  │
│  ✗ Nothing calls it     ✗ Nothing compiles it                │
└──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                           │
              ┌────────────┴────────────┐
              │                         │
              ▼                         ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐
│   iOS Platform Layer    │ │  Android Platform Layer  │
│                         │ │                          │
│  Objective-C++ (.mm)    │ │  JNI + Java/Kotlin       │
│  CocoaPods / Podspec    │ │  CMake + Gradle          │
│  Xcode build system     │ │  NDK build system        │
│                         │ │                          │
│  Gets runtime from      │ │  Gets runtime from       │
│  RCTCxxBridge           │ │  JavaScriptContextHolder │
│  (+ Bridgeless shim)    │ │  via JNI                 │
└─────────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────┘
```

Figure 1: One C++ core, two platform-specific wiring layers. The C++ code is portable — the build systems and initialization code are not.


This is the "platform wiring" — the two per-platform layers that compile your C++, bridge the language gap, and call `install()` at the right time.

4543	
4544	
4545	## Decoding the Trace: Frame by Frame
4546	
4547	Let's walk through every piece, mapping each symbol to the concept from the series that explains it.
4548	
4549	
4550	### The Signal
4551	
4552	
4553	```
4554	signal 11 (SIGSEGV), code 1 (SEGV_MAPERR), fault addr 0x7b1a4fe000
4555	```
4556	
4557	
4558	- SIGSEGV — the process tried to access memory it doesn't own. The OS killed it.
4559	
4560	- SEGV_MAPERR — the fault address isn't mapped into the process's virtual address space. This distinguishes use-after-free (address was freed) from null dereference (`0x0`). The fault address `0x7b1a4fe000` is non-null and high — it was once valid memory.
4561	
4562	- This is a use-after-free: the memory at that address was deallocated, then accessed.
4563	
4564	
4565	### The Crashing Thread: AudioEncoder
4566	
4567	
4568	```
4569	#00  memcpy+180                          (libc.so)
4570	#01  audio::TxRingBuffer::push(...)      (libaudio.so)
4571	#02  audio::CaptureEncoderThread::processFrame(...)  (libaudio.so)
4572	#03  audio::CaptureEncoderThread::run()  (libaudio.so)
4573	#04  __pthread_start(void*)              (libc.so)
4574	```

4576	Reading bottom-up (the call stack grows downward):
4577	
4578	
4579	Frame
4580	What it is
4581	Learned in
4582	
4583	
4584	`#04 __pthread_start`
4585	The OS thread entry point. A `std::thread` was created, and this is where it begins execution.
4586	Part 8
4587	
4588	
4589	`#03 CaptureEncoderThread::run()`
4590	The encoder's main loop — `while (running_) { processFrame(); }`. A long-lived background thread, not a one-shot task.
4591	Part 9
4592	
4593	
4594	`#02 processFrame(CaptureQueue&)`
4595	Pulls a raw PCM frame from the lock-free SPSC queue (between the audio capture callback and the encoder), runs noise suppression and Opus encoding, then pushes the encoded packet to the transmit ring buffer.
4596	Part 9
4597	
4598	
4599	`#01 TxRingBuffer::push(uint8_t const*, unsigned long, long)`
4600	Writes encoded audio bytes into the ring buffer. The arguments: a pointer to the Opus packet, its size, and a timestamp.
4601	Part 9, Part 3
4602	
4603	
4604	`#00 memcpy+180`
4605	The actual instruction that faulted. `push()` called `memcpy` to copy bytes into the ring buffer's backing array — but that array no longer exists.
4606	Part 3
4607	
4608	
4609	### The Main Thread: Idle
4610	
4611	
4612	```
4613	#00  __epoll_pwait   (libc.so)
4614	#01  android::Looper::pollOnce(int)   (libutils.so)
4615	```
4616	
4617	The Android main thread is blocked in `epoll_pwait` — waiting for events (touch, vsync, Looper messages). It has nothing to do with the crash. This rules out UI-related causes.
4618	
4619	
4620	### The JS Thread: Garbage Collecting
4621	
4622	
4623	```
4624	#00  facebook::hermes::vm::Hades::collectOG()
4625	#01  facebook::hermes::vm::GCBase::finalizeUnreachableObjects()
4626	#02  std::__ndk1::shared_ptr::~shared_ptr()
4627	#03  audio::AudioPipelineHostObject::~AudioPipelineHostObject()
4628	#04  audio::TxRingBuffer::~TxRingBuffer()
4629	#05  facebook::jsi::Runtime::PointerValue::invalidate()
4630	```
4631	
4632	The destruction sequence follows a chain: GC triggers finalization, finalization triggers the destructor cascade. Here's what each frame means:
4633	
4634	
4635	Frame
4636	What it is
4637	Learned in
4638	
4639	
4640	`#00 Hades::collectOG()`
4641	Hermes's old-generation garbage collector (`Hades` is the GC algorithm name, `OG` = old generation). This runs periodically on the JS thread. The GC found an unreachable object and is cleaning it up.
4642	Part 1
4643	
4644	
4645	`#01 finalizeUnreachableObjects()`
4646	The Hermes GC determined this HostObject is no longer reachable from JavaScript. No JS variable holds it. Finalization begins.
4647	Part 1
4648	
4649	
4650	`#02 shared_ptr::~shared_ptr()`
4651	The `shared_ptr` reference count hit zero. The last owner — the JSI runtime — released its reference.
4652	Part 6
4653	
4654	
4655	`#03 AudioPipelineHostObject::~AudioPipelineHostObject()`

4657	Part 5
4658	
4659	
4660	`#04 TxRingBuffer::~TxRingBuffer()`
4661	The ring buffer's destructor. Its backing array is freed. **This is the moment the memory at `0x7b1a4fe000` becomes invalid.**
4662	Part 3
4663	
4664	
4665	`#05 PointerValue::invalidate()`
